tone_statements.citation: Abuov, Zhoumaghaly [Абуов, Жумагали]. 1994. The phonetics of Kazakh and the theory of synharmonism. UCLA Working Papers in Phonetics 88: 39-54.
tone_statements.quote: Dzhunisbekov (1987) has demonstrated that Kazakh and other Turkic languages with synharmony are typologically distinct from intonation languages, such as English, as well as from tone languages, such as Chinese. ... Although synharmony does not operate across word boundaries, it interacts with the prosodic system of Kazakh by allowing stress to assume a predominantly syntactic role in the language. Languages with synharmony have rhythmic stress; they differ fundamentally from both stress/intonation languages and tone languages.

tone_statements.summary: Kazakh classed as neither a tone nor a stress/intonation language: synharmony defines the word, stress is phrasal (rhythmic-group-final), following Dzhunisbekov; no pitch/tone analysis given.

sources.citation: Özçelik, Öner. 2015. 'Stress' or 'intonational prominence'? Word accent in Kazakh and Uyghur. Turkic Languages 19(2): 163-192. doi:10.13173/TL/2015/2/163 (author-posted copy, oozcelik.pages.iu.edu).
sources.quote: Regular prominence is word-final and moves right with suffixation (almá, alma-lár, alma-lar-ím, alma-lar-ɨm-dá:); production experiment with Kazakh speakers finds final syllables significantly longer (duration the correlate, not intensity/pitch), analysed as a single weight-sensitive iamb at the right edge ([LL(LH́)]). Adds: 'at least in some varieties of Kazakh, syllable weight is crucial ... heavy syllables attract stress' (kép.ka, ʃe.gírt.ke, der.ba.zá:, sa.rɨm.sák), and pre-stressing suffixes (negation -MA, question -MA, copula/agreement) give exceptional non-final stress.

sources.citation: Özçelik, Öner. In press. Kazakh phonology. In L. Johanson et al. (eds.), Encyclopedia of Turkic Languages and Linguistics. Leiden: Brill. 6-7 pp. (author preprint, oozcelik.pages.iu.edu).
sources.quote: 'As with most Turkic languages, accent in Kazakh falls on the final syllable of a prosodic word. As such, each time a suffix is added to a word, accent appears to move to the right' (almá ... alma-lar-ím-dá). Notes accented syllables bear greater duration, apparent root exceptions align with syllable weight, and pre-stressing suffixes (negation, question particle, adverbial -ʃA, copula/person agreement).

sources.citation: Bazarbaeva, Z. M. [Базарбаева, Зейнеп М.]. 2008. Kazakhskaia intonatsiia [Казахская интонация / Kazakh intonation]. Almaty: Daik-Press. 281 pp.
sources.note: Treats word prosody typologically: the possible 'prosodic dominant' of the word is accent (word stress), synharmonism, or tone; for Kazakh (and Turkic generally) the dominant is synharmonism (four synharmonic word types), while Kazakh word stress is fixed on the final syllable, immobile and non-contrastive; no lexical tone is attributed to Kazakh (tone appears only as an alternative dominant of other language types). Secondary/programmatic rather than an instrumental tone study.

tone.quote: В казахском языке словесное ударение фиксированное (неразноместное, неподвижное), падает на последний слог слова, поэтому не выполняет смыслоразличительную, формо-различительную функции, не является фактором порождения редукции гласных в составе казахскго слова. [...] В связи с такой неполиаспектностью функции словесного ударения в казахском языке просодической доминантой казахского слова (и слова других тюркских языков) является сингармонизм, который в зависимости от участия языка и губ подразделяется на четыре типа
tone.locator: body section on prosodic dominants of the word (article pp. 895-913; page of the passage not established from the HTML text)
tone.translation: In Kazakh, word stress is fixed (not free, not mobile); it falls on the last syllable of the word and therefore performs no meaning-distinguishing or form-distinguishing function and is not a factor causing vowel reduction within the Kazakh word. [...] Given this non-multifunctional role of word stress in Kazakh, the prosodic dominant of the Kazakh word (and of the word in other Turkic languages) is synharmonism, which, depending on the participation of the tongue and lips, is divided into four types
tone.n_tones: None: no lexical tone attributed; word-prosodic dominant = synharmonism
